data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The non-expert panel's apparent superiority is often a baseline-rate artifact: when outcomes are highly skewed, a checklist with high item sensitivity but low specificity induces the panel to 'track' the right answer at the aggregate level while individual judgments remain uninformative.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the task base rate is balanced (e.g., 50/50), a base-rate artifact cannot explain panel accuracy; a genuine gain is more plausible.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If panel calibration is evaluated per-judgment (e.g., Brier score) rather than aggregate accuracy, the base-rate artifact is exposed because overconfidence on negatives inflates the score.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Base-rate tracking: In a skewed task (e.g., 95% negative), a checklist designed to catch positives flags many false positives. A panel majority vote suppresses these false positives if the errors are random, yielding high apparent accuracy matching the base rate. This is mere compliance with the checklist's structure, not a reliability gain.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
